title: The Peshtigo Fire: America's Deadliest Wildfire That History Forgot
summary: On October 8, 1871, the same night as the Great Chicago Fire, a firestorm in northeastern Wisconsin killed between 1,200 and 2,400 people -- at least five times more than Chicago -- and remains the deadliest wildfire in recorded history.

content.intro: Everyone knows about Mrs. O'Leary's cow. Almost no one knows about Peshtigo. On the night of October 8, 1871, while the Great Chicago Fire was burning its way into American legend, a vastly more lethal catastrophe was unfolding 250 miles to the north in the Wisconsin woods. The Peshtigo fire killed at least five times as many people as the Chicago fire. It generated winds of 110 miles per hour and temperatures exceeding 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit. It threw rail cars and houses into the air. It destroyed 17 communities and erased every local record of its own death toll. And then it was almost entirely forgotten, overshadowed by a more photogenic disaster in a more famous city.

sections.title: Tinder-Dry and Burning Already
sections.body: The summer of 1871 had been brutally dry across the upper Midwest. Slash-and-burn land clearing -- the standard method for making way for farms and railroad lines -- had left the Wisconsin and Michigan forests littered with debris. Small fires smoldered constantly; the smoke was so thick that steamship captains on Lake Michigan had trouble navigating. Peshtigo, a town of about 1,700 people in northeastern Wisconsin, sat surrounded by pine forests and sawdust from its woodenware factories. The town was, in effect, made of fuel. On the evening of October 8, an eastward-moving cold front pushed through the region, dramatically increasing wind speeds. The scattered slash-and-burn fires merged, feeding on each other and on the parched landscape. What erupted was not a forest fire. It was a firestorm.

sections.title: Nature's Nuclear Explosion
sections.body: A firestorm is a fundamentally different phenomenon from an ordinary wildfire. As described by historians Gess and Lutz, superheated flames advance on winds exceeding 110 miles per hour, with temperatures above 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit. The fire creates its own weather system, generating updrafts powerful enough to spawn fire whirls -- rotating columns of flame that survivors described as tornados. These fire whirls threw rail cars and entire houses into the air. The Reverend Peter Pernin, an eyewitness, described the fire leaping across the Peshtigo River using bridges and upward air drafts, burning both sides of the town simultaneously. Citizens fled into the river itself, into wells, into any body of water they could reach. Some drowned. Others died of hypothermia in the frigid water while fire raged on both banks. In addition to Peshtigo, 16 other communities were destroyed that night.

sections.title: A Death Toll Lost in the Ashes
sections.body: An accurate count of the dead was never possible because the fire destroyed all local records. The 1873 Report to the Wisconsin Legislature listed 1,182 names of dead or missing residents, but estimates range from 1,200 to 2,400 -- making the Peshtigo fire the deadliest wildfire in recorded history and likely deadlier than the 1889 Johnstown flood. In Peshtigo alone, a town of 1,749 people, more than 350 bodies were buried in a mass grave because no one remained to identify them. The small village of Williamsonville in Door County lost 57 of its 76 residents and was never rebuilt. That same night, fires also ravaged Holland and Manistee in Michigan, across Lake Michigan, and Port Huron at the southern end of Lake Huron. The coincidence of so many fires on a single night even spawned a comet hypothesis: speculation dating to 1883 that fragments from Biela's Comet caused the simultaneous ignitions. The real explanation required no extraterrestrial help -- just dry conditions, scattered existing fires, and a strong cold front.

sections.title: The Peshtigo Paradigm
sections.body: William B. Ogden, the politician and factory owner who had built Peshtigo's industry, returned to rebuild the town. Progress was slow. Many buildings, including the woodenware factory, never reopened. Today Peshtigo has roughly 3,500 residents. A memorial was dedicated on October 8, 2012, at the bridge over the Peshtigo River, and the Peshtigo Fire Cemetery is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. But the fire's most enduring legacy may be military. The specific combination of topography, wind conditions, and ignition sources that produced the firestorm became known as the "Peshtigo paradigm," and American and British military planners studied it during World War II to learn how to recreate firestorms during bombing campaigns against cities in Germany and Japan. The deadliest wildfire in American history became a blueprint for incendiary warfare.

content.flightContext: Located at 45.05°N, 87.75°W in northeastern Wisconsin, along the Peshtigo River near where it empties into Green Bay. The burn area extended across much of the southern Door Peninsula and adjacent parts of Michigan's Upper Peninsula. From altitude, the landscape has long since regrown -- second- and third-growth forest covers the region. The Peshtigo Fire Cemetery and memorial are near the river bridge in town. Nearest airports include Green Bay-Austin Straubel International Airport (KGRB) about 40 miles to the south and Menominee-Marinette Twin County Airport (KMNM) roughly 10 miles to the north. Tornado Memorial County Park, on the site of destroyed Williamsonville in Door County, lies to the east.
